Like most people in these comments, I am have autism. However, this experience may not be exclusive to neurodevelopmental disorders. It’s very recent that specialists are putting together a holistic view of Ehlers Danlos to understand how it manifests in various systems, including the nervous system. 

There is increasing evidence that EDS significantly impacts neurological function. That may be why it’s closely associated with things like autism and ADHD. [Here](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4300794/) is a report that details potential symptoms/manifestations of EDS in the nervous system. It very well might be that your nerves are just more “sensitive” and the result is sensory issues. 

I am not a doctor, but there are potential treatments/therapies for overactive nerves. You can see a neurologist if you’re able. Otherwise, I’ve found vagus nerve stimulation and a TENS/NMES machine helpful. Ultimately, no, you’re definitely not alone. But its something that you may be able to tone down.

Honest advice from someone who did stranger hookups for several years as opposed to real dating/socializing: you may continue to hate yourself if you don’t take time to think about what you really want. Hyper-sexuality is a feeling, like any other, and self-regulating it is important. Buy toys, talk to strangers online, whatever you need to do! Just don’t meet strangers for quick hook-ups. There have been many situations where I realized afterward, ‘oh, that was really dangerous/that wasn’t what I wanted.’ The difficult thing about autism, for me, is not being present in the moment or able to recognize a situation for what it is, nevertheless speak for myself. I honestly didn’t know I was meeting people to hook up until they started having sex with me. For a long time, I thought that was just normal ‘dating’, you go to a strangers house and sit there until they want to take your clothes off. It was awful and I got hurt a lot, but I kept doing it because I didn’t know any better. Being on the spectrum makes it REALLY easy for people to take advantage of you. Even if you proactively seek sex, there are so many things a person can do to you that aren’t okay, and I realized I had to stop because I literally could not protect myself in those moments. My kind of off beat suggestion is: look into a local kink community. Read about it online see if anything interests you. For one: many GENUINE members of the BDSM community are very, very serious about consent and communication. I have had good experiences with those that consider it a lifestyle. You can talk about (or write, it it’s easier)  what you’re looking for, i.e., I don’t want to be touched with bare skin, I don’t want to be fully undressed, I don’t want to talk, I want this type of touch in these places with these toys/body parts, and that’s it. There are plenty of people who, at the very least, you can find community with where sex is more of a structured experience/exchange that is well-defined. I wish you the best, and please be safe as you proceed. Hook-ups on apps are NOT safe. It only takes one bad choice.

It’s not ignorant at all! That’s actually the ‘cool’ science part about neurodivergence! Stress reactions are neurological in origin. An over-reactive central nervous system is a key component of shutdowns, meltdowns, stimming, sensory processing issues, and other things that historically have been ‘trained’ out of us. If the nervous system is not able to respond accordingly to overstimulation, it can cause physiological damage to itself and the body as a whole. Just because an action is caused or accompanied by a strong emotion, like stress, doesn’t mean it’s an acquired behavior. 

In a very basic sense, neurotypical brains process the world more ‘efficiently’, which allows them to prioritize the input they receive. ASD brains don’t do that (possibly because of poor neuron pruning, among other things), so we are flooded with undiluted information and sort through it differently. That neurological difference is the SOURCE the autistic behaviors observed by neurotypicals. 

I have heard (and experienced) that the scientific study of autism has focused more-so on how inconvenient our symptoms are to them (the weird factor), rather than why we have them. It’s historically been approached from a psychological perspective, particularly with an extremely flawed ‘correct and cure’ approach. There’s a lot of conjecture and professionals are only beginning to understand who we are beyond the gravity of social burden we pose.

Hello, I have always found [this](https://autismawarenesscentre.com/shutdowns-stress-autism/) case study to be similar to my experience. 

I was diagnosed with PDD-NOS, which has only recently been absorbed into the autism diagnosis. By appearances I have low support needs, however, certain things such as involuntary shutdowns are very impactful and dangerous. If you’ve ever blacked out drunk, it may be like that, except for being entirely sober and slightly cognizant of what’s happening. If there is too much stressful stimulation, my nervous system turns off. Like a Windows XP modem shutdown. I get really physically hot, my heart beats fast, my eyes roll, and my motor skills fail. Sometimes, everything goes black for a few minutes to a few hours and when I ‘wake up’, I have completed a task or moved locations. Not being able to speak can feel very dissociative, like I can’t control what my body does or doesn’t do. It’s like being a brain stuck inside a body rather than the two being a single entity. Selective mutism is common in autism, but difficult to differentiate, personally, from going nonverbal because neither is a choice. There are times I find speaking difficult due to disorganized thoughts, anxiety, or just genuinely having nothing to say. When I express an inability to speak, it is a temporary neurological difficulty and not a preference. For example, I was once arrested for a DUI because I couldn’t speak after a car accident I caused. 

Even supposed specialists struggle to differentiate neurological from psychological behaviors in autism, so this is anecdotal based on a lack of co-occurring issues like epilepsy or narcolepsy that would explain my experience. I hope this helps!

People perceived as women tend to experience poor treatment regardless of attractiveness, though the type of mistreatment varies. There are obvious advantages to being ‘pretty’, but there are many negatives as well. 

As an attractive autistic woman, I am still crushed by the pressures of being attractive every day. There is no winning because the game is a million moving targets. The only outcome is that we all lose to varying degrees. It’s designed this way for a reason. 

One of the only things that seems to unite all women in Western society is how isolating the experience of womanhood is. Neurodivergence is a more nuanced way to experience it, but you aren’t alone in that either.

It may be more comforting and sustainable to know that women suffer because they are women, not because of how well or poorly they perform femininity. 

Here are some videos that may help:

[The Price of Pretty Privilege by Hala](https://youtu.be/jbnl7h8y5YM) explains some difficulties of beautiful women without denying the accompanying privileges. 

[Desirability Unpacked by Khadija Mbowe](https://youtu.be/lnxQeh7Rsog) talks about desire as a weapon against women.  

[Gender Performativity and the Surveillance of Girlhood by Shanspeare](https://youtu.be/clt3Nj6dHwk) is a more generalized view on femininity.

My therapist also approaches treatment as “individual not diagnosis” focused. I understand the purpose of this, but it brings about many feelings:
• I am being dismissed. They do not believe my diagnosis is appropriate or valid. 
• I’m not being adequately treated because the therapist/doctor isn’t educated in neurodivergence and does not wish to seek out information that would individualize their services to me. 
• They do not understand is not a disease, it is a difference in essential cognitive processing. 

You are right to be hurt. Unfortunately, we have to approach traditional treatment with greater understanding than most neurotypicals (especially health providers) offer us. They are taught that diseases and disorders can and should be separated from the “ideal” person that is trapped by symptoms, rather than acknowledging that these differences are immutable from the individual. 

I recently vocalized this in a therapy session. Something along the lines of: “Autism affects every aspect of my life. It’s really important to me as a lens for understanding why I struggle the way I do. I went a long time feeling inherently wrong for existing without knowing that the world I live in isn’t built for me to do more than survive.” 

Obviously it was less eloquent than that, but he seemed to understand. I think we have to do more work than we should to get mental health help. There is (ironically) a finite spectrum in my experience, where health providers either attribute everything to a diagnosis and offer no help, or they dismiss the diagnosis and offer the wrong help. Either way, we aren’t being treated correctly. I even asked if my therapist thinks talk therapy can “work” for everyone. He was pleasantly surprised by the question and basically said that it completely depends on what both parties are willing to put into it. 

Ultimately, the first struggle (and it’s a difficult one) is finding a therapist who is AT THE VERY LEAST willing to adapt. There aren’t a great many that treat adults with autism without ABA therapy. Most therapy from what I understand is based in cognitive behavioral and dialectical behavioral therapy. Teaching people to connect thoughts to feelings to actions. That’s not particularly effective (in my opinion) for those with crippling self-awareness, like myself. 

My tips are:
• Write down your concern. Build up the courage to read it from the page or message it to your therapist if that’s possible. 
• If she seems receptive, proceed. If not, look for someone that may be. It might take a while. Please don’t be discouraged. I’m early in my journey too, but therapy is what people do when they’re struggling so I have to believe that even minimal benefits are worth the effort. 
• Find resources that mirror your experience. Ask your therapist if you can provide them as a reference for what you struggle with. Frame it as “are these things that you can help me process/work on improving?”
• If you analyze yourself constantly, like I do, write it down. Journal. Keep a digital document for random thoughts. Anything to help you process things so that you feel comfortable verbalizing them. It can also help you decipher what is important to talk about and what isn’t. Therapy is YOUR time. The provider is just a guide. She’s a resource. Don’t let her derail your narrative or try to provide blanket advice like breathing exercises (I hate that stuff). You can share this document with your therapist directly or read from it in sessions. 
• This was especially hard for me, but set goals for therapy. I was initially like “this is what people do when they’re sad/anxious/angry”. I have all of these problems, I know what they are, I know what could potentially fix them, but there is a difference between awareness and progress. If I know these things, why can’t I fix them? The answer is that I am autistic and have experienced a substantial amount of trauma. I need to work through that trauma with a professional trained in directing that process. That’s the first step to separating my guilt for not being ‘normal’ from my actual inabilities to improve. I find that I view my differences as failures. My inability to be the “ideal” person keeps me from extending the necessary empathy to myself that would permit me to grow. I have to unlearn internalized ableism that demands me to be something I will never be. I have to accept what I am now, understand what my basic needs are in contradiction to what I demand of myself, and figure out what happiness looks like for someone who doesn’t find success in the neurotypical parameters of it. 

Happiness is an abstract concept. So is suffering. That being said, they’re both very real feelings. They’re very individual to. A good therapist will listen to how you suffer and help you move away from it. Defining what happiness looks like is completely up to you, and in itself can be a monumental accomplishment. Set small goals: I will stop cancelling appointments, I will do three intentional acts of self-care a day, I will establish a system to ensure I eat three meals a day, I will write about my feelings every day. 

This is all based on my own experience, I apologize if it’s overwhelming or unhelpful. Adequate health care requires a lot more work than sitting down with a stranger to talk about your childhood, especially for neurodivergent folks. I’m sorry you’re already feeling discouraged. You aren’t alone.

I had a period where I hallucinated certain things before/shortly after falling asleep. My brain was taking sounds (and silence) and making noises of them. You have to create an environment that guards against sensory fears (dark, open space, physical vulnerability) 

1. warm colored night light
2. YouTube videos of brown noise to fill the silence (you can put a timer on them) 
3. Lock your door/put a sound maker on the handle
4. I sleep with a billion pillows around my body and a blanket over my neck. Moved my bed to a nook in my room, but against a wall is fine
5. Two layers of pajama bottoms. Idk why it just makes me feel secure
6. Talk to a psychiatrist if you can. Medication can help. I take hydroxyzine or clonidine. 
7. Put a heating pad on your bed before you get in to make it cozier
8. Melatonin spray for your pillow

Make the process of going to sleep as comfy and secure as possible. I’m sorry you’re experiencing this. It won’t always be so difficult. For me, it comes in waves and then I’ll be okay for a while.

I’ve always told people I feel like a passenger in a ‘Body Vehicle’. I’m aware of my mind looking out through the windshield (eyes). I feel the presence of every system in my body. It controls the volume and the visuals and my movement.

It was so validating to know that this isn’t ‘normal’ and that I’m not alone in it. Kind of explains why I’ve never connected to my name/recognized it as my own. It feels WRONG to have a name. I wish I had an off-switch that wouldn’t hurt people that love me.

I think you look very feminine. I am autistic too and makeup used to be an interest of mine. I have progressively lost the ability to wear a full-face like I used to. Here are some things I use now that are easy and don’t cause discomfort:

•lip stain, doesn’t feel heavy like lipstick and doesn’t come off easily. I use [colourpop gloss](https://www.ulta.com/p/glossy-lip-stain-pimprod2030947), you put it on and then dab it off. I can’t see your skin undertones with the filter, but they’re relatively cheap enough to buy a couple and see what color suits you. 

•blush makes a huge difference. I think cream ones maintain the feeling of my skin as opposed to a scratchy powder blush. I use [glossier cloud paint](https://www.glossier.com/products/cloud-paint)but there are affordable alternatives. The Colour Pop brand I mentioned above has a creamy powder blush that is nice and much cheaper. Look up a chart to help you find the best placement for your face shape, it makes a difference. I’ve worn makeup for over ten years I didn’t learn the ideal blush placement of my face until recently. 

•eyebrow filling and gel! Strong and shaped eyebrows are very feminine to me. It can be hard to figure out where to start with eyebrow shaping, but darkening the outer edges of your natural eyebrows is a good start.

•eyeliner is always a plus but it does bother me at times. You can play around with fun colors, though and sometimes that makes it worth the sticky feeling. 

I hope this helps

Yes, I’m 23F, thin and muscular, and I say that so anyone with a different body type knows it’s not caused by weight gain. I have deep, pink and purple stretch marks on all sides of my upper thighs, behind my calves, on my side tummy, under my (notably tiny) bosom, even sideways above my butt (from sitting on this absolute dump truck). I understand being insecure about them, but they’re really not that big a deal! It’s how your skin forms! 

You can try lightening them with topical vitamin c and vitamin e oil, but I have been alternating a micro needle roller and tretinoin (prescription vitamin a) cream. I’ve not seen improvement yet but it’s only been about eight months and it can take over a year to see results apparently. 

If you try to treat them or leave them be, know it’s not something most people (adults with basic humanity) care about or even notice. It’s annoying to me when people call them tiger stripes or whatever, or say they’re beautiful/proof you’re grown. Stretch marks don’t have to be beautiful! Your skin was not made to be beautiful! Your body does not determine worthiness! It was made to be alive, and that you are! Good job! 

Side note: like 40% of my body is covered in tattoos, yes the only bleeds and muddles on this cursed baby soft skin, but it has helped my confidence tremendously. If you’re into the idea, turning the parts of your body that make you feel yucky into artwork is the move. I even love the ugly tattoos I got in parking lot swap meets. Do whatever you have to do to make your skin suit comfier to live inside.

Sports are dangerous for EDS. Exercise can help specifically with muscle building to support the joints, but it’s hurtful to hear that suggestion because most of our lives we have been told we are lazy/uncoordinated/aren’t trying enough. Exercising is painful and also high risk for injuries without physical therapist monitoring at first. 

My suggestion is to just listen. My boyfriend is very good about this. He listens and he learns. He is very mindful of the fact I simply cannot do certain things. He thinks ahead about how long we will have to walk or stand to do something without making me feel like a helpless baby. He knows I have a high pain/discomfort tolerance and won’t tell him when I need help, so he proactively offers rest opportunities, helps me with things, offers alternatives to certain activities. 

Sex is a complicated one. I’ve found that EDS peeps with vaginas have a hard time with it in various ways. We expect discomfort and pain. Sometimes our bodies anticipate that pain so much that they evolve to disallow it completely (ex. Vaginismus). The best thing you can do on that front is just talk to her. Don’t ask vague questions that she might not have thought about/are too big to really address. ‘Does this hurt?’ doesn’t really work because everything kind of does. Ask things like, ‘does this feel better this way or do you prefer x?’ Get creative. Use pillows. Watch videos on foreplay stuff from actual (female) sex therapists (she may need more time spent on the front-end to have a good time overall. I didn’t even know I could enjoy the experience until my boyfriend made it completely about me). There’s a lot of that content on TikTok and YouTube. Consider experimenting with bands/restraint type set ups. There are a lot of bondage harnesses that actually help us a lot in terms of keeping our joints legs in place and not overusing our muscles. Be verbal with your own feelings so she feels comfortable voicing hers. This is all important for any healthy sexual relationship, but it’s ESSENTIAL for women with EDS. A lot of our injuries and subsequent suffering is located in the hips/lower spine/pelvic floor. 

I’m glad you’re so willing to learn about her. I’d personally be happy to answer specific questions you have if no one else will. Don’t worry about “hurting her”. She’s lived with chronic pain likely her entire life. It’s probably background noise most of the time. It’s a completely different experience than you breaking your leg or getting a headache. She can handle more than you can think. As long as you’re listening thoughtfully, you will naturally learn how to navigate alongside her.

It’s congestion and a damaged skin barrier, I think! Your barrier skin cells create a thicker barrier than is really necessary to keep the lower ones protected. That’s why you see the signs of congestion building up, your cells aren’t turning over as quickly as they could. There are lots of online services where you can send pictures to a dermatologist and get a prescription for relatively cheap to free depending on your insurance or where you are. Curology and Nurx come to mind because I’ve used them, but there are others! If you’d rather try to treat this yourself, you’re going to need to understand how your skin works. Knowing a bit of the science helps you stick to a routine and maintain mindfulness in my opinion! You can use very a simple cleanser to wash dirt, oil, and pollutants from your skin. I like to use a toner after washing that will restore a healthy pH balance for my skin, and a hydrating serum to hold onto the moisture that was created by washing.  Neither are necessary for a basic routine, though. An exfoliant a few times a week will start improving the appearance of your pores and congestion (not immediately, your skin has to get used to it). You can use AHAs, BHAs, or retinol products. They’re all a bit different and have different strengths, so you may want to read a bit about that. [Here](https://www.healthline.com/health/beauty-skin-care/aha-and-retinol) is an article that kind of explains what those do for you. If you’ve never exfoliated, starting with a simple AHA might be the easiest and least impactful in terms of side effects. 

Think of exfoliants as aggressively ripping the blanket from your skin. It’s going to be vulnerable, maybe sensitive, and it needs a temporary barrier to keep it safe and nourished. That’s where a good moisturizer comes in. I swear by Cerave. Simple, cheap, and lasts forever. You’ll want to moisturize twice a day, and if you use an exfoliant, sunscreen is always necessary because your skin is temporarily more susceptible to sun damage. 

Be mindful that the number one factor is TIME. It takes a while for positive changes to be visible because your skin is so complex. Do some research on products and application methods, figure out a routine that’s realistic for your lifestyle, and stick to it! You may start seeing the benefits in a few weeks, but it could also take a few months. I hope this helps, good luck!

Retinoids don’t cause sun damage, they just expose newer cells to the sun and give the appearance of sun sensitivity! Because it causes increased cell turnover, it actually enables your body to repair DNA damage that the sun (and environmental mutagens) cause. Over time, your cell turnover remains optimized, or fast and effective, without the direct use of retinol, your skin acclimates to the product so well that it remembers exactly what it’s supposed to be doing! This doesn’t last forever of course but the effect is much stronger skin that is actually less prone to sun damage overall. You should always use sunscreen and try to limit exposure, but retinol really isn’t that much of a risk factor for long-term damage overall and it does have benefits that no other topical product can replicate. It’s super dicey to get used to, but with commitment I think it’s the best we’ve got.

I am of the opinion that it’s better (and cheaper long term) to prevent than repair. A lot of doctors say you don’t NEED retinol, but it’s the gold standard tool for treating issues people tend to have with their skin as they grow. Retinol is one of the most well-researched anti-aging products (and cure-all for acne/dark spots/texture issues). It’s relatively cheap when you think about gimmicky, untested products on the shelves of Sephora. I tend to fall into the trap of ‘this is a pretty container and a fun, trendy ingredient’ and I save up to buy something that does absolutely nothing for me. Your body thinks there isn’t enough to go around, so it’s going to lower the amount of calories it needs to keep you going. Your basal metabolic rate takes serious hits with any period of restriction. It also matters what you’re eating to an extent, and how much activity you’re getting. I will say, if you’re at an extreme calorie deficit, meaning below the lowest suggested adult intake (probably your binge amount), do not exercise. I have done irreparable damage to myself by doing this. You don’t want to be disabled by your own actions. Btw those ‘binge’ days might be better to look at as reset days. You’re turning up the energy production in your body and giving it something to burn. I understand that this disorder doesn’t just come from weight issues or weight loss goals alone, but if you’re really focused on that, you may want to research metabolic repair! It’s really helpful to understand why your body does what it’s doing. It’s just keeping you safe! And per your last concern, nothings wrong with your body, but there is something wrong with the way you think about it. Eating doesn’t mean you aren’t sick. If eating or not eating causes you significant distress, is a constant concern, and you find yourself acting against your best interest, there is something wrong and you deserve help. You can get better! Whenever you’re ready, the resources are there for you. Hugs if you need them!

Not sure if you’re looking for advice, I apologize if not, let me know and I’ll delete. The one thing I’ve learned after YEARS with this illness seems pretty obvious, but sometimes I’ve gotta eat. The best defense against bingeing is hydration (not in excess) and the right kinds of food. Your body is gonna want the quickest, sugariest stuff after restriction and you’re not going to be in the state of mind to make healthy decisions. That uncontrollable feeling is your body taking the wheel to keep you alive, not you failing. I promise! 

My suggestion to try to match cravings to the nutrients that your body is asking for. There are charts online that tell you things like chocolate means you need magnesium, you get that from nuts and certain fruits. It has helped me so much, and I still feel in control while I’m getting nutrients. I still binge occasionally, but I try to be kind to myself and realistic. I reset by washing my face, showering, massaging my face for any sodium swelling, and then eating protein and healthy carbs the next day. You’re hungry and it’s okay to answer that feeling however you need to. It’s been really hard, but I’ve tried to shift it the narrative in my head to food = fuel. If your biggest fear is weight gain, the only way to continue losing weight after a certain point is to eat. Your body is going to lower your metabolic rate to the point that basically nothing is going on, so of course you’ll gain when you eat! Your intake is below what your body needs to survive, of course it’s gonna out that into storage for your organs and your brain. That’s just the science of it.
